What if we hosted a blog space for moderators of subverses, a place where mods could openly discuss their though though processes, bounce future ideas around, and generally interact with the community.

Have the button for the blog right next to Hot/New/Top Etc, so it's consistent.

The Blog would be a place where rule changes could be publicly discussed, and it would have a comments section just like on the main subverse page. The main idea would be to free up the subverse from meta posts from the moderator team, and give them a place for all rule changes and things that is permanently stickied.
Why make it a part of the site fully? How many are actually going to use it? If they want to do that, they could just make posts, or a small subverse to deal with it.

Hopefully we'll see how many people are actually interested.

The main idea was to keep the links centralised, if the mods made a small sub linking to it would theoretically constitute brigading, and it's designed to clear up the post stream for content- not rule changes.

I think it would be a nice tool to differentiate the site from competitors, as well as encourage good mod behaviour by giving them a space to explain things in a permanent fashion. With a post, it will eventually get buried, but a blog-like section is very heavily archived, allowing users to look back to see previous decisions and rule changes.

Just an idle thought while I was reading the latest news on the Trans-Pacific Partnership... if the entire world started trading freely, with no protectionism whatsoever, how would things change? If you need hand-wavey justification for this scenario I suppose you could imagine that aliens showed up and forced the Earth to immediately change its economic model or be destroyed.
If all trade tariffs and subsidies all around the world were eliminated, how would the world change?

Wouldn't comparative advantage just take over the world economy? America's manufacturing industry would shrink drastically with only the high-quality and specialty manufacturers surviving, as low-cost manufacturing countries take over a larger market share of labor-intensive goods. Remember when the US got pissed at China for dumping an obscene amount of tires into the US because it was killing US manufacturers? Well that would happen again, except the government wouldn't do anything and it would happen for many more goods as well. Bikes, TVs, toasters, shirts, and any other manufactured good that doesn't require large capital investment would cease to be made in the US.

I don't see the service market being affected nearly as much as the goods market. We (the US) would see investment opportunities arise in previously banned markets, such as Iran, South Korea, and Cuba. The developing world would continue to develop their own service industries.

I wrote this from the perspective of an American university student, but feel free to swap in any developed nation for the US in my comment. I don't see the broad concepts changing based on which developed nation we use.
I don't see a problem with the Chinese effectively subsidizing American goods. Dumping, by definition, means selling goods below cost. So, if they want to pay for Americans to have tires--let 'em.

In a word: consolidation

The same kind of consolidation we saw in the United States when the banks were deregulated.
